title: Oxidation Numbers and Balancing Redox Equations

blocks.text: In a covalent compound no electrons are actually handed over, so how can you say anything has been oxidised? Chemists solved this with a bookkeeping device: pretend every bond is fully ionic and count. That pretend charge is the oxidation number, and it works every time.

blocks.title: Oxidation number
blocks.text: The oxidation number of an atom is the charge it would carry if all the bonds in the species were completely ionic, with each shared pair assigned to the more electronegative atom. It is written with the sign first, as +2 or -2, to distinguish it from an ionic charge such as 2+.

items: Any element in its free, uncombined state has an oxidation number of 0. This includes O2, Cl2, S8 and metallic Na
A simple monatomic ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge, so Na+ is +1 and S2- is -2
The oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to zero
The oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion add up to the charge on the ion
Group I metals are always +1, group II always +2 and aluminium always +3 in compounds
Hydrogen is +1 in its compounds, except in metal hydrides such as NaH where it is -1
Oxygen is -2 in its compounds, except in peroxides such as H2O2 where it is -1, and in OF2 where it is +2
Fluorine is always -1 in compounds, since nothing is more electronegative

blocks.title: Oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion
blocks.prompt: Determine the oxidation number of chromium in the heptaoxodichromate(VI) ion, Cr2O7 2-.

steps.text: Let the oxidation number of chromium be x. There are two chromium atoms, contributing 2x in total.
Oxygen is -2, and there are seven oxygen atoms, contributing 7 x (-2) = -14.
The sum must equal the charge on the ion, which is -2.
This is why the ion is named heptaoxodichromate(VI); the Roman numeral in the name is the oxidation number.

blocks.answer: Chromium has an oxidation number of +6

blocks.markdown:
## Balancing by half equations

Split the reaction into an oxidation half and a reduction half, balance each separately, then combine.

1. Balance all atoms other than hydrogen and oxygen.
2. Balance oxygen by adding H2O to the side that needs it.
3. Balance hydrogen by adding H+ (in acidic solution).
4. Balance the charge by adding electrons to the more positive side.
5. Multiply the two half equations so that the electrons cancel, then add them.

For the manganate(VII) ion in acid:

MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O

Check the charge: on the left -1 + 8 - 5 = +2, and on the right +2. Balanced.

blocks.title: Combining two half equations
blocks.prompt: Combine the half equations MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O and Fe2+ -> Fe3+ + e- into a single balanced ionic equation.

steps.text: Count the electrons. The reduction half uses 5 electrons but the oxidation half releases only 1, so they do not yet cancel.
Multiply the whole oxidation half equation by 5: 5Fe2+ -> 5Fe3+ + 5e-.
Now both halves involve 5 electrons, so they will cancel when added.
Add the two equations and cancel the electrons: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ -> Mn2+ + 4H2O + 5Fe3+.
Check the atoms: 1 Mn, 4 O and 8 H on each side, and 5 Fe on each side.
Check the charge: left is -1 + 8 + 10 = +17; right is +2 + 0 + 15 = +17. Balanced.

blocks.title: Charge must balance too
blocks.text: An ionic equation is only correct when both the atoms and the total charge balance. Checking the charge takes five seconds and catches almost every mistake in the number of electrons or hydrogen ions.

points: Free elements have an oxidation number of 0, and simple ions have the value of their charge.
Oxidation numbers sum to zero in a compound and to the ionic charge in a polyatomic ion.
Oxygen is normally -2 and hydrogen +1, with peroxides and metal hydrides as the exceptions.
A rise in oxidation number is oxidation; a fall is reduction.
Balance half equations with water, hydrogen ions and electrons, then scale so the electrons cancel.
Always check that both atoms and total charge balance in the final equation.
